about: The tour: one landing plan followed across the whole screen, step by step, run by src/sightline/Tour.tsx. It is told in four chapters: the problem, one landing answered, the plan changing (a later date, other sites, a miss), and why to trust it and how to hand it on. Wherever the story moves to another part of the screen, the step arrives with the control a visitor would press ringed, and the first Next presses it for them (`then`, or `press` for a control whose press computes something), so the reader learns the way there. A visitor reading alone steps through each step's `line`, two sentences on the card that stand by themselves; Listen, or Play through, gives `say`, the spoken line, rendered once in Scout's voice by scripts/tour-voice.mjs --tour=five. Every figure in a card or a spoken line is on screen at that step.
name: Scout's tour

voice.from: Google Cloud Text-to-Speech, the voice Scout speaks with on the site (en-US-Chirp3-HD-Leda), rendered once from each step's "say"

steps.title: A hard place to land
steps.line: A lander needs the Sun for power and Earth for a direct radio link. At the Moon's south pole both only skim the horizon, so the hills decide when each is in view.
steps.say: This is the Moon, seen from above its south pole. A lander there needs two things from the sky: the Sun, for power, and Earth, for a direct radio link. It is nothing like Earth: the Moon turns once a month, and near its pole the Sun and Earth never climb. They skim the horizon, so the hills decide when each is in view.

steps.title: Plan a landing
steps.line: Press Plan a landing: the front page is the Moon to watch, and this button starts a plan. Choose where, a listed site or any coordinates, and when, in UTC.
steps.say: The front page is the Moon to watch. Plan a landing starts a plan, and a plan begins with two choices. Where: a listed site, from Apollo to NASA's commercial landers, other countries' landers and future targets, or any point on the Moon, by its coordinates. And when: a date and hour, in UTC. Ours is Connecting Ridge, on the sixth of May 2027.

steps.title: What it must survive
steps.line: Press the mission to see what it must survive: 14 days, at most 24 h dark or 24 h of radio silence. Advanced can ask that Earth's center clear the skyline by 2° or 5°.
steps.say: The third choice is the mission: what it must survive. A short stay is fourteen days, with at most a day of darkness, at most a day of radio silence, the Sun and Earth in view at landing, and ground no steeper than ten degrees. In view means any part of the disc above the skyline. That is generous for a radio link, so Advanced can ask for Earth's center to stand two or five degrees clear.

steps.title: Does it fit?
steps.line: Does it fit those limits? The answer comes first, fits, fits with little margin or does not fit, and why. Under it: the Sun's elevation, each body's share of the mission, the slope.
steps.say: So, does it fit? The answer comes first. This landing does not, and Sightline says why: the Sun is down for ninety-five hours and Earth is out of view for a hundred and sixty-nine, against a limit of a day each. Under it are the numbers: the Sun's elevation, a key measure for power, and its share of the mission; Earth, the same way; and the ground's slope.

steps.title: What the lander sees
steps.line: So why does it not fit? Press Surface to stand at the site: the Sun and Earth are low over the real skyline, each with the time until it sets.
steps.say: So why does it not fit? One window faces the Sun, the other Earth, over the real skyline, traced from NASA's laser-measured terrain. Both are low, and each counts down: sunset in five and a half days, Earthset in seven. Seen from the Moon, Earth stays in one place; near the pole that place is the skyline, so here it sets.

steps.title: Hour by hour
steps.line: Now run the 14 days forward. Gold is the Sun, blue is Earth, green is both: the gaps are why this landing fails. Play it, or step out to a year.
steps.say: Now run the mission forward. Gold is the Sun, blue is Earth, green is both. The frame marks the fourteen days, and the gaps inside it are the verdict's reasons: the Sun gone for four days, Earth gone for the whole second week. Play it, or step back to a day, a month or a year. Over a year the pattern shifts: the Moon has seasons too.

steps.title: The date slips
steps.line: Launch dates slip, and this one has to. One press adds the next landing that fits beside the first: the same site, on 22 June.
steps.say: Now the real problem: launch dates slip. Sightline names the next landing that fits. One press, and it is in the plan beside the first, as scenario B: the same site, on the twenty-second of June, nearly seven weeks later, with a green verdict. In separate tools, that means starting again in each one.

steps.title: Another option
steps.line: Now the plan holds two scenarios, A and B: each letter is a site and a landing hour. Press + for another, up to four; − on a letter drops it.
steps.say: The plan now holds two options, each with a letter: A, the first landing, and B, the later one. A letter is one scenario: a site and a landing hour. The plus adds another, up to four. There: scenario C. Change its site or date, and the whole screen answers for it. The minus on a letter drops it, and Undo brings it back.

steps.title: Another site, same date?
steps.line: Would another site save 6 May? Press Compare: C and D, two more sites near the pole on that date, do not fit either. A star marks the best in each row.
steps.say: Waiting is one answer. Would moving be another? Compare sets the scenarios side by side: A failed, B is the later date, and C and D are two other sites near the pole on the original date. Neither fits, though one is sunlit for two thirds of the mission and the other for a seventh. A star marks the best in each row; there is no blended score.

steps.title: Every site, every month
steps.line: Press Planner to see every listed site against every month. In May 2027 no site at the pole has a landing that fits; in June, Connecting Ridge has three days.
steps.say: So was May ever possible? The Planner steps back to every listed site against every month, counting the days with a landing that fits. In May 2027, none of the four ridge sites at the pole has one. In June, Connecting Ridge has three. A site that never fits says which limit blocks it.

steps.title: What if it misses?
steps.line: Press Landing accuracy: B fits on its aim point, but no lander comes down exactly there. Of the landings within reach, 38% fit; aim 44 m away, and 60% do.
steps.say: We chose B. But no lander comes down exactly on its mark. B fits on its aim point, and yet, of the touchdowns within about a hundred meters of it, only thirty-eight percent would. Landing accuracy shows what goes wrong in the rest, and offers a better aim: forty-four meters away, where sixty percent fit. Near the pole, a few meters matter.

steps.title: NASA's maps and tools
steps.line: Press Site and Layers to look at the ground itself, under NASA's own maps. Every plan also opens in Quickmap, Moon Trek and JPL Horizons.
steps.say: Now look at the ground itself. Three views show the same hour: the whole Moon from orbit, the site close up, and the surface. Layers puts NASA's own maps over the ground: photos, steep ground, permanent shadow, temperature. And every plan opens in Quickmap, Moon Trek and JPL Horizons, so anyone can check.

steps.title: Can it be trusted?
steps.line: Press Guide for the proof: every number is checked against NASA three ways, with JPL Horizons, NASA's sunlight map and dated photos. It also says what Sightline cannot tell you.
steps.say: Can it be trusted? Every number is computed from public NASA data by our own code, then checked against NASA three ways. The positions are compared with JPL Horizons at every hour. The long-run sunlight, with NASA's own map. And the model, with dated photos taken from orbit. The Guide tells that story for a first-time visitor, and says plainly what Sightline cannot tell you.

steps.title: Ask Scout
steps.line: Or just ask: press Scout. He answers in plain words from the same data, and never writes a number himself: the server fills in every figure.
steps.say: Or just ask. Scout takes a question in plain words and looks the answer up in the same data the screen uses. He is an AI, and he is never allowed to write a number himself: the server fills in every figure, so what he says matches what you see.

steps.title: Hand it on
steps.line: Hand it to your team: Brief writes the scenario on show out in full, to print, and Share makes a link to the same plan. Then try Canada's rover mission, or start your own.
steps.say: Last, hand it on. A plan is for a team: Brief writes the scenario on show out in full, to read or print, and Share makes a link that opens the same plan for whoever gets it. Planners get every hour as a table and NASA's links; a class gets the Guide. Try a real mission, Canada's utility rover, or start planning your own.

prepare.about: What the later steps read (the four sites Compare sets side by side, the ground's maps, the terrain Landing accuracy works on, the Guide's checks), asked for quietly once the tour starts, so that each step is ready when the visitor or a presenter arrives at it. All are files the steps would ask for anyway.
